questions.stem: A client who is 24 weeks pregnant receives a new prescription for oral tetracycline. Which action is most appropriate before the first dose?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer the medication because fetal dental effects are limited to first-trimester exposure and the client is already beyond that period.","B":"Clarify the prescription only if treatment is expected to exceed 21 days because repeated short courses do not affect developing teeth or skeletal tissue.","C":"Give the tetracycline with a calcium-containing meal because binding the drug in the intestine prevents clinically important fetal exposure during pregnancy.","D":"Clarify the prescription before administration because tetracycline use during the last half of pregnancy can affect developing teeth and fetal bone."}}
questions.rationale: Tetracycline-class labeling warns that use during tooth development, including the last half of pregnancy, can cause permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia. Tetracycline-class drugs also can affect developing bone. At 24 weeks, the nurse should clarify the prescription before administration.
questions.source_detail: Tetracycline-class use during the last half of pregnancy can affect tooth development; fetal skeletal effects are also a concern.

questions.stem: A client has taken high-dose omeprazole for several years and now reports persistent watery diarrhea plus hip pain after a low-impact fall. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Both findings warrant evaluation because PPI therapy is associated with C. difficile–associated diarrhea and long-term/high-dose use with fracture risk.","B":"Evaluate the diarrhea, but the hip symptom is unrelated because osteoporosis-related fracture risk is associated with H2 blockers rather than proton-pump inhibitors.","C":"Evaluate the hip symptom, but C. difficile is unlikely because PPI-associated diarrhea risk occurs only during concurrent antibiotic therapy at present.","D":"Continue the current PPI unchanged because diarrhea and musculoskeletal discomfort are expected chronic effects that do not require reassessment of long-term therapy."}}
questions.rationale: Current omeprazole labeling warns that PPI therapy may be associated with increased risk of C. difficile–associated diarrhea. Long-term and multiple-daily-dose PPI therapy may also increase risk of osteoporosis-related hip, wrist, or spine fractures. Both findings warrant evaluation rather than automatic dose escalation.
questions.source_detail: Warnings include C. difficile–associated diarrhea and osteoporosis-related fracture risk with long-term/multiple-daily-dose PPI therapy.

questions.stem: A client taking felodipine extended-release drinks grapefruit juice every morning. Which teaching is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Separate grapefruit juice from felodipine by at least four hours because the interaction occurs only when both reach the intestine at the same time.","B":"Replace grapefruit juice with orange juice only if the felodipine dose is increased because all citrus juices produce the same CYP3A4 inhibition at usual doses.","C":"Grapefruit can markedly increase felodipine exposure and intensify blood-pressure effects; avoid it or clarify regular grapefruit use with the prescriber.","D":"Limit grapefruit to a small serving with breakfast because clinically meaningful changes in felodipine exposure occur only with several large servings per day."}}
questions.rationale: Felodipine is metabolized by CYP3A4. Current labeling reports that grapefruit juice can increase felodipine AUC and peak concentration by more than twofold, potentially increasing blood-pressure effects. The client should avoid or clarify grapefruit use rather than deliberately combining it with the drug.
questions.source_detail: Grapefruit juice increased felodipine AUC and Cmax by more than twofold; CYP3A4 inhibition can increase pharmacologic effects.

questions.stem: A client taking sertraline develops agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, and hyperreflexia soon after a second serotonergic medication is added. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are most consistent with uncomplicated anxiety because serotonin toxicity generally causes isolated sedation without autonomic or neuromuscular findings.","B":"The findings are concerning for serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening reaction that requires prompt clinical evaluation and medication review.","C":"The findings indicate an anticholinergic syndrome because excessive acetylcholine activity typically produces diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and tremor.","D":"The findings are an expected transient combination effect that can be observed at home unless a localized rash or mild gastrointestinal symptom appears."}}
questions.rationale: Sertraline and other SSRIs can precipitate serotonin syndrome, particularly when combined with other serotonergic drugs. Labeling lists agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, and hyperreflexia among characteristic findings. This pattern requires prompt evaluation rather than reassurance or attribution to simple anxiety.
questions.source_detail: Serotonin syndrome is potentially life-threatening; risk rises with other serotonergic drugs and may include agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, and hyperreflexia.

questions.stem: A client taking digoxin has a potassium level of 3.0 mEq/L, while the serum digoxin concentration remains within the laboratory reference range. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A reference-range digoxin concentration excludes clinically meaningful toxicity, so the potassium result can be addressed without reviewing the digoxin regimen.","B":"Hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk but does not change myocardial sensitivity to digoxin unless the serum digoxin concentration exceeds the reference range.","C":"Potassium replacement should be delayed until a repeat digoxin concentration is elevated because normal-range digoxin prevents electrolyte-related toxicity.","D":"Hypokalemia increases susceptibility to digoxin toxicity, so symptoms, rhythm, renal function, electrolytes, and the medication regimen require prompt review."}}
questions.rationale: Current digoxin labeling states that hypokalemia can predispose a patient to digoxin toxicity and that toxicity can occur at lower serum digoxin concentrations. Clinical findings, rhythm, renal function, electrolytes, and the medication regimen therefore matter even when the measured digoxin concentration is within a laboratory reference range.
questions.source_detail: Hypokalemia and other electrolyte abnormalities may predispose to digoxin toxicity; assess serum electrolytes and renal function.
